newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge blocks deportation of Nicaraguans.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge blocks deportation of Nicaraguans.

text.p: A U.S. federal judge on Tuesday issued a preliminary injunction to prevent the deportation of thousands of Nicaraguans and other immigrants in three states, at least until a trial scheduled for early next year.
The ruling effectively prevents the U.S. government from sending home Nicaraguans who have lived in legal limbo since coming to the United States during the 1980s civil war in their country.
Ira Kurzban, a lawyer for the immigrants, hailed the ruling, calling it a "major victory."

"This decision will not only have a direct and immediate impact on tens of thousands of people here, but will influence the fate of hundreds of thousands of Salvadorans, Guatemalans, Nicaraguans and others throughout the United States," Kurzban said in a statement.
"It is an historic and monumental decision."

U.S. District Judge James Lawrence King, in a ruling that affects immigrants in Florida, Georgia and Alabama, set a trial date of January 5, 1998 on whether to issue a permanent injunction in the case.

On May 14, King issued a temporary restraining order preventing deportations until he could fully hear arguments from lawyers who claimed as many as 40,000 Nicaraguans and other immigrants had been illegally stripped of their immigration rights under the government's interpretation of new laws.
On June 12 King said he could not immediately rule on a request for an injunction, effectively allowing the restraining order to expire and permitting the United States to resume deportations.

The Immigration and Naturalisation Service then vowed there would be no mass deportations and said it would await King's ruling. On Tuesday, an INS spokesman said the agency was "reviewing the matter."

The new immigration laws enacted in April left tens of thousands of Miami immigrants, primarily Nicaraguans, living in fear although they had been living legally in the United States and paying taxes for years. Lawyers said many pulled their children out of school and were moving from house to house to avoid deportation.

"These are families that mind their own business, that have integrated themselves (into society)... They're not a threat and they don't jeopardise the national security of the United States," said Jose Lagos, public relations director for Fraternidad Nicaraguense, a Nicaraguan community organisation that was one of the plaintiffs.

Seeking to stop the deporatations and gain permanent residency, the plaintiffs filed suit. Thousands of Nicaraguans have also demonstrated in the streets of Miami, among them uniformed ex-guerrillas who fought in the U.S.-backed Contra army against Nicaragua's leftist Sandinistas during the country's eight-year civil war.
